title: Stokes' Theorem
body:
[[Green's Theorem]] lifted out of the plane. The circulation around the boundary curve of a surface
equals the [[Flux]] of the [[Curl]] through that surface.

$$
\oint_{\partial S} \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{F})\cdot d\mathbf{S}
$$

$S$ is any orientable surface, $\partial S$ its boundary curve, and the two orientations must agree
by the right-hand rule: thumb along the surface normal, fingers curl the way the boundary is
traversed.

## The consequence worth having

**The right side depends only on $\partial S$.** So any two surfaces sharing a boundary give the
same answer, and you may replace an unpleasant surface with a convenient one: a hemisphere by the
flat disk beneath it, say. That substitution is most of what the theorem is used for in practice.

Two immediate corollaries:

- If $S$ is **closed** it has no boundary, so the flux of a curl through it is zero. Which is
  $\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{F}) = 0$ arriving from the integral side
- If $\nabla\times\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{0}$ on a simply connected region, every closed-loop
  circulation is zero, so $\mathbf{F}$ is a [[Conservative Vector Field]]. This is the proof of
  that test

## One family of theorems

| Theorem | Left (boundary) | Right (interior) |
|---|---|---|
| [[Fundamental Theorem of Calculus]] | $f(b)-f(a)$, two endpoints | $\int_a^b f'\,dx$ |
| Fundamental theorem for line integrals | $f$ at the endpoints of $C$ | $\int_C \nabla f\cdot d\mathbf{r}$ |
| [[Green's Theorem]] | circulation round $\partial D$ | curl over the plane region |
| **Stokes' Theorem** | circulation round $\partial S$ | curl through the surface |
| [[Divergence Theorem]] | flux through $\partial E$ | divergence over the solid |

Every row says *the integral of a derivative over a region equals the original function evaluated
on the boundary*. That is the through-line of the whole course, and in the language of differential
forms all five rows are literally the same theorem, $\int_{\partial\Omega}\omega = \int_\Omega d\omega$.

## Related

- [[Green's Theorem]]: the flat case, with $S$ a region of the $xy$-plane
- [[Divergence Theorem]]: the other three-dimensional one, flux rather than circulation
